_comment: English-only focus description prose for the South Korean Cold War tree; narrative description layer, distinct from numeric reward tooltips.
COLDWAR_KOR_developmental_state_desc: Park directs the ministries through the Economic Planning Board. Rapid execution rests on a contested presidential mandate. The Economic Planning Board can align credit, foreign exchange and ministry targets, but its authority still depends on Park's contested mandate.
COLDWAR_KOR_yushin_desc: Concentrate executive authority and replace direct presidential competition with controlled institutions. Under Yushin, the president would be chosen indirectly by the National Council for Unification, while presidential appointments shaped one-third of the Assembly.
COLDWAR_KOR_constitutional_drp_desc: Retain conservative development policy under a competitive constitutional settlement. A civilian DRP settlement would preserve electoral competition and conservative development, asking Park's administration to accept a legislature with a real bargaining role.
COLDWAR_KOR_emergency_decrees_desc: Emergency powers accelerate decisions while surveillance and repression widen the legitimacy crisis. Decree rule puts policy in the Blue House and security organs, narrowing the space for courts, assemblymen, students and labor to challenge state action.
COLDWAR_KOR_assembly_bargain_desc: Accept legislative bargaining and scrutiny in return for a more durable civilian mandate. Assembly negotiation offers the ruling party a broader civilian basis, in exchange for hearings, amendments and opposition leverage over legislation.
COLDWAR_KOR_presidential_administration_: A professional cabinet gives either constitutional settlement an administrative foundation. Career officials and the Economic Planning Board would translate presidential priorities into budgets and investment schedules across ministries.
COLDWAR_KOR_chaebol_compact_desc: Channel policy credit through major business groups; concentrated guarantees deepen financial exposure. Directed loans and guarantees favor established conglomerates able to deliver large projects, while concentrating repayment risk and bargaining power in a few firms.
COLDWAR_KOR_competitive_credit_desc: Distribute development finance to smaller exporters, sacrificing conglomerate economies of scale. Banks would assess smaller exporters and suppliers on performance, broadening access to capital while giving up some scale and coordination enjoyed by chaebol.
COLDWAR_KOR_export_targets_desc: Reward firms that meet overseas sales targets, at the cost of leverage and workplace pressure. Export quotas reward firms that earn foreign exchange, but managers may meet them through wage restraint, overtime and heavier borrowing.
COLDWAR_KOR_subcontractor_guarantees_des: Enforce contracts and protect provincial suppliers from dominant buyers. Enforceable payment terms give smaller parts makers and regional workshops leverage against dominant buyers, even when large exporters prefer flexible contracts.
COLDWAR_KOR_planning_board_desc: The Economic Planning Board would arbitrate ministry investment requests, set export benchmarks and report progress to the cabinet. Its stronger coordinating role brings ministries under a common development schedule.
COLDWAR_KOR_mobilized_villages_desc: Use state-led village mobilization to deliver rural development and extend presidential influence. Saemaul-style campaigns combine state materials, village labor and official targets; delivery can improve roads and farms while binding local leaders to central priorities.
COLDWAR_KOR_rural_cooperatives_desc: Give cooperatives control over rural credit and priorities, limiting central mobilization. Cooperative credit committees let farmers set more of their own investment priorities, diluting the county office's role in directing village projects.
COLDWAR_KOR_performance_grants_desc: Reward successful villages, accepting uneven access and political dependence. Matching grants reward villages that complete approved works, favoring organized communities and leaving poorer or less connected settlements behind.
COLDWAR_KOR_village_accounts_desc: Local audits improve trust while slowing central allocation. Published village accounts give residents a way to question spending and project selection, though consultation takes time from centrally scheduled works.
COLDWAR_KOR_balanced_provinces_desc: Extend transport links beyond the dominant southeastern corridor. New links beyond the southeastern export corridor would help provincial producers reach ports and markets, spreading access beyond the favored industrial belt.
COLDWAR_KOR_dynastic_presidency_desc: A DRP successor would carry forward the governing machine and industrial programme. Selecting continuity through the ruling party could reassure senior officials, while opponents may see the arrangement as personal rule in civilian dress.
COLDWAR_KOR_civilian_handover_desc: Prepare a constitutional transfer, trading presidential discretion for legitimacy. A negotiated transfer would ask the DRP leadership to accept electoral uncertainty in return for a more credible civilian succession.
COLDWAR_KOR_parliamentary_government_des: A governing New Democratic Party restores parliamentary opposition rights and independent political association. NDP leaders would restore assembly debate, opposition organization and association rights, while inheriting ministries built around presidential direction.
COLDWAR_KOR_parliamentary_republic_desc: Build a cabinet responsible to the Assembly; coalition bargaining constrains executive speed. A cabinet dependent on Assembly confidence gives party blocs influence over policy, trading rapid executive decisions for coalition durability.
COLDWAR_KOR_checked_presidency_desc: Keep an effective presidency subject to term limits and parliamentary scrutiny. Direct presidential authority remains, but term limits and assembly scrutiny make executive continuity answerable to voters and legislators.
COLDWAR_KOR_coalition_committees_desc: Make committee oversight permanent despite the administrative cost. Standing committees let governing and opposition members examine legislation before floor votes, with additional bargaining across a divided Assembly.
COLDWAR_KOR_constitutional_court_desc: Judicial review strengthens rights while imposing an additional administrative burden. Constitutional review gives citizens and legislators a forum to contest executive acts, requiring judges and clerks independent of cabinet direction.
COLDWAR_KOR_civil_service_review_desc: Replace political appointments with accountable professional administration. Merit review and transparent appointments would weaken party patronage inside ministries, while requiring new standards for promotion and discipline.
COLDWAR_KOR_market_conservatives_desc: Open credit allocation and restrain preferential guarantees, accepting slower conglomerate expansion. Private lenders and open competition would replace some directed guarantees, improving access for entrants but leaving favored conglomerates to finance expansion on stricter terms.
COLDWAR_KOR_social_conservatives_desc: Preserve private enterprise while underwriting social compromise. Employers, labor representatives and conservative legislators would negotiate a limited social settlement that protects private ownership while funding basic security.
COLDWAR_KOR_open_tenders_desc: Transparent procurement benefits new suppliers at an administrative cost. Published bids invite provincial firms to compete for public work, though ministries must spend more effort checking qualifications and contract performance.
COLDWAR_KOR_pension_contributions_desc: Contributory benefits broaden security but reduce resources available for immediate investment. Payroll contributions would link benefits to formal employment, extending security gradually while placing a new charge on workers and employers.
COLDWAR_KOR_regional_compromise_desc: Fund an industrial project in Honam to reduce the regional imbalance. A Honam industrial project would answer complaints that public investment and export infrastructure favored the southeast, without immediately leveling regional capacity.
COLDWAR_KOR_civilian_security_desc: Subject security agencies to civilian warrants and legislative oversight. Warrants and assembly reporting place intelligence operations under civilian law, limiting political surveillance while preserving investigation of genuine security threats.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_compromise_desc: Retain parts of the security apparatus, accepting continued civic distrust. The NDP would retain some experienced security officials and operating capacity, accepting that unresolved abuses may continue to trouble opposition and students.
COLDWAR_KOR_democratic_conservatism_desc: Consolidate a constitutional conservative government with a credible international reputation. Conservative rule gains standing from regular elections and lawful opposition, while preserving alliance ties and a market-oriented development programme.
COLDWAR_KOR_reform_mandate_desc: A reform government reopens civic politics and reviews political imprisonment. A reform cabinet would reopen civic association and review political detention, facing resistance from officials whose authority grew under emergency rule.
COLDWAR_KOR_ys_civilian_authority_desc: Assert civilian authority over the officer corps, accepting a difficult transition in command. Kim Young-sam's civilian leadership would challenge the political role of officers, requiring command changes that may unsettle the armed forces.
COLDWAR_KOR_dj_people_economy_desc: Link civil rights to household welfare and regional inclusion. Kim Dae-jung's people-centered programme links civil liberties with household welfare, placing redistribution and regional fairness alongside industrial growth.
COLDWAR_KOR_financial_disclosure_desc: Require disclosure and curb hidden political finance. Disclosure rules expose party donations and corporate ties to public scrutiny, narrowing the channels through which political finance can remain hidden.
COLDWAR_KOR_negotiated_cleanup_desc: Secure business cooperation through phased accountability. A phased settlement would enlist business groups in reform while sequencing investigations, preserving investment cooperation but delaying full accountability.
COLDWAR_KOR_real_name_accounts_desc: Require accountable financial records and transparent corporate ownership. This is an alternate precursor, not Kim Young-sam’s 1993 real-name-finance reform. Identifiable bank records would make corporate ownership and political finance easier to trace, challenging long-standing reliance on anonymous accounts.
COLDWAR_KOR_corporate_transition_desc: Preserve investment momentum while deferring part of the cleanup. Gradual restructuring protects orders and employment at major firms, but postpones scrutiny of cross-shareholdings and politically directed credit.
COLDWAR_KOR_ys_civil_coalition_desc: Kim Young-sam would join parliamentary opponents, civic organizers and conservative defectors in a common reform front. Each partner would retain its own organization, so keeping the coalition together requires continuing negotiation.
COLDWAR_KOR_ys_consolidation_desc: Civilian appointment rules would make senior offices accountable to elected ministers and legislators. Replacing personal patronage with reviewable procedures takes time and can provoke officials who benefited from informal access.
COLDWAR_KOR_broad_welfare_desc: Build broad social protection with a substantial recurring public commitment. National insurance would pool risks across households rather than leave protection to employers, requiring a stable public contribution as enrollment expands.
COLDWAR_KOR_targeted_welfare_desc: Target vulnerable households while keeping the fiscal commitment narrower. Means-tested support concentrates resources on the poorest households, but local officials must identify need without turning relief into patronage.
COLDWAR_KOR_national_health_cover_desc: Extend coverage to groups left outside employment-based protection. Coverage beyond large-company payrolls would reach small businesses, farmers and informal workers, demanding a wider network of clinics and financing.
COLDWAR_KOR_regional_equalization_desc: Direct assistance to excluded regions, accepting administrative complexity. Transfers to poorer provinces would support services and employment outside Seoul and the southeast, though central agencies must measure need fairly.
COLDWAR_KOR_dj_civil_coalition_desc: Kim Dae-jung's alliance would bring regional constituencies and civic associations into parliamentary opposition. A shared platform broadens its reach, though it asks local leaders to accept compromises beyond their immediate priorities.
COLDWAR_KOR_dj_consolidation_desc: National labor mediation would give unions and employers a regular forum for disputes over pay and production. Officials must sustain that process through strikes and economic pressure rather than rely on emergency settlement.
COLDWAR_KOR_sixth_republic_desc: Consolidate competitive institutions under either reform leader. A civilian constitution would establish competitive institutions under either reform leader, making rights and executive limits rules of state rather than campaign promises.
COLDWAR_KOR_democratic_alliance_desc: Use democratic credibility to deepen the US alliance while accepting closer external influence. A rights-based government could reassure Washington and deepen security consultation, while making alliance expectations part of domestic political debate.
COLDWAR_KOR_reform_nordpolitik_desc: Explore northern diplomatic openings while keeping decisions under civilian oversight. Civilian officials would test commercial and diplomatic channels with socialist states, preserving the alliance while reducing exclusive reliance on bloc politics.
COLDWAR_KOR_military_cabinet_desc: A military-led government relies on discipline and command networks rather than a civilian mandate. A military cabinet draws authority from command cohesion and national-security claims, but faces a legitimacy deficit among civilian institutions and urban society.
COLDWAR_KOR_fifth_republic_desc: Institutionalize Chun’s controlled presidency and civilian party vehicle. The 1980 constitution would preserve a strong indirect presidency and appointed representation, placing civilian parties beneath executive authority.
COLDWAR_KOR_managed_liberalization_desc: Accept a negotiated constitutional opening while retaining conservative institutions. A limited opening can ease censorship and party restrictions while the governing conservative coalition retains substantial control over the pace of change.
COLDWAR_KOR_press_consolidation_desc: Centralize media and political supervision at a lasting cost to credibility. Licensing, editorial pressure and security review bring broadcasters and newspapers closer to government priorities, at the expense of public credibility.
COLDWAR_KOR_june_declaration_desc: Restore direct presidential competition; this changes election rules rather than installing a predetermined winner. Direct election answers the June 1987 movement's central demand, but the opposition's divided candidates leave the outcome to voters.
COLDWAR_KOR_professional_officers_desc: Promote professional competence while funding a better paid officer corps. Career education and predictable promotion strengthen military professionalism, accompanied by better-supported personnel and training institutions.
COLDWAR_KOR_stabilization_first_desc: Restrain inflation and implicit guarantees through a difficult industrial adjustment. Tighter credit and reduced guarantees would restrain inflationary pressure, asking factories and workers to absorb a difficult period of adjustment.
COLDWAR_KOR_industrial_continuity_desc: Support strategic enterprises through the downturn, accepting renewed financial exposure. Continued support for heavy industry protects capacity in steel, shipbuilding and machinery, but renews the state's exposure to indebted groups.
COLDWAR_KOR_industrial_rationalization_d: Industrial expansion has left some business groups carrying debts that their earnings cannot sustain. A coordinated restructuring would concentrate finance on viable production, asking creditors, managers and workers to share the losses rather than preserve every established commitment.
COLDWAR_KOR_export_recovery_desc: Coordinate export recovery through wage restraint and public support. Export finance and wage discipline could restore overseas competitiveness, shifting adjustment costs toward workers and firms serving the home market.
COLDWAR_KOR_civil_administration_desc: Put routine administration in professional civilian hands. Civilian ministries would resume ordinary budgeting and service delivery, displacing officers from roles better suited to professional administrators.
COLDWAR_KOR_hanahoe_compact_desc: Preserve loyal command networks, accepting political interference and civic distrust. Protecting officer-club ties can steady command relationships, but makes promotions appear political and deepens civilian suspicion of military influence.
COLDWAR_KOR_retire_political_officers_de: Remove political commands, accepting temporary disruption in exchange for public trust. Retirement terms give politically active officers a route out of command, accepting vacancies and a temporary loss of experienced leadership.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_continuity_desc: Retain coordinated security control under military-linked leadership. Military-linked officials retain intelligence coordination and internal security authority, strengthening control while blurring the line between defense and politics.
COLDWAR_KOR_civilian_promotions_desc: Make promotion accountable to civilian institutions rather than private officer clubs. A civilian review of promotions would reduce club influence over assignments, asking senior officers to accept a slower and more formal process.
COLDWAR_KOR_olympic_republic_desc: A more open international presence can connect the Republic with markets and diplomatic partners beyond its established security relationships. Seoul must invest in that engagement while accepting that foreign attention also brings closer scrutiny of political conditions at home.
COLDWAR_KOR_roh_nordpolitik_desc: An elected Roh government explores diplomatic recognition and northern trade. Roh Tae-woo's elected government would pursue trade and recognition with socialist states, expanding diplomatic options without abandoning the United States alliance.
COLDWAR_KOR_conservative_merger_desc: Negotiate an elite conservative coalition. No opposition party or incumbent is transferred without political agreement. A merger among conservative parties could pool legislative strength, but only negotiated concessions can resolve disputes over leadership and regional bases.
COLDWAR_KOR_social_democratic_cabinet_de: Kim Chul’s small socialist tradition becomes a governing coalition through a credible democratic opening. A Kim Chul-led social-democratic government would turn a small reform tradition into a governing coalition after a substantial democratic opening.
COLDWAR_KOR_universal_insurance_desc: Make social protection a national entitlement financed by a broad public commitment. Universal benefits make entitlement independent of a worker's employer, requiring a broader tax and contribution base than a limited insurance scheme.
COLDWAR_KOR_contributory_welfare_desc: Build a narrower, employment-funded system with lower immediate public spending. Employment-linked contributions build benefits alongside formal payrolls, keeping public commitments narrower but excluding many informal workers at first.
COLDWAR_KOR_rural_health_desc: Extend protection to farming and informal households outside large-company employment. County clinics and portable coverage would extend care to farming households beyond the large firms that anchor employment-based systems.
COLDWAR_KOR_portable_benefits_desc: Carry benefits across employers while accepting a complex contribution system. Portable entitlements follow workers between employers, improving security in a mobile labor market while complicating contribution records.
COLDWAR_KOR_independent_unions_desc: Legalize independent collective organization; exporters must accommodate bargaining. Independent union registration gives workers a lawful bargaining channel outside the state-linked federation, requiring employers to negotiate production terms.
COLDWAR_KOR_public_credit_desc: Keep credit allocation accountable to public institutions rather than conglomerates. Public lending institutions would set development priorities through accountable mandates, balancing industrial expansion against the risk of political loan allocation.
COLDWAR_KOR_social_market_industry_desc: Preserve private industry under binding employment and wage agreements. Private firms retain ownership while negotiated wage and employment rules share productivity gains with workers.
COLDWAR_KOR_cooperative_industry_desc: Support producer cooperatives at the cost of capital and administrative effort. Producer-owned firms would pool capital and decisions, widening worker voice but making investment and expansion harder to coordinate.
COLDWAR_KOR_works_councils_desc: Give labor representation in company decisions, exchanging speed for coordination. Elected workplace councils give employees a standing role in production decisions, slowing unilateral management changes in exchange for cooperation.
COLDWAR_KOR_balanced_development_desc: Support industrial employment outside established corporate centers. Industrial incentives outside Seoul and the southeast would create new employment centers, though private firms may still favor established supply chains.
COLDWAR_KOR_socialist_alliance_desc: Maintain an independent democratic left and cultivate foreign social-democratic contacts. The democratic left would seek ties with foreign socialists while keeping Korean policy under domestic party and parliamentary control.
COLDWAR_KOR_neutral_peace_desc: Negotiate international neutrality while maintaining a funded defense. Treaty withdrawal needs a separate accepted settlement. Neutrality would require credible guarantees from abroad and continued readiness at home; neither alliance obligations nor defense costs disappear by declaration.
COLDWAR_KOR_labour_republic_desc: Consolidate a democratic labor settlement without adopting Pyongyang’s political system. A labor-centered republic can protect collective organization while retaining plural elections and separate Southern constitutional institutions.
COLDWAR_KOR_student_cabinet_desc: A radical civic coalition turns campus mobilization into accountable government; this is alternate history. Civic Cabinet institutions must survive beyond the student protests that helped bring them to power, while competing organizers retain distinct demands.
COLDWAR_KOR_campus_pluralism_desc: Protect universities and open debate while funding a wider educational mission. Autonomous faculties and student associations can debate competing social programmes, with public grants tied to clear academic standards.
COLDWAR_KOR_national_service_schools_des: Link civic service to technical education, diverting young people from civilian careers. Technical classes and civic service would prepare young people for public works and local administration, but compulsory service narrows individual choice.
COLDWAR_KOR_technical_scholarships_desc: Widen technical education instead of relying only on elite institutions. Scholarships would widen access to engineering and applied sciences beyond elite families, tying education spending to future industrial capacity.
COLDWAR_KOR_community_service_desc: Expand a compulsory service programme with practical training and a wider obligation. Local service placements combine training with public works, but a compulsory model risks narrowing individual choice and labor supply.
COLDWAR_KOR_civic_charter_desc: Make the civic coalition constitutional rather than a permanent campus emergency. A charter protects organized student and civic activity through ordinary law, replacing temporary mobilization with durable political rights.
COLDWAR_KOR_student_cabinet_public_accou: Published accounts would show how public loans and investment are allocated. Students, legislators and local groups could use the records to question insider access and assess whether funded projects serve broader needs.
COLDWAR_KOR_independent_left_desc: A southern socialist coalition claims independence from both blocs; it is an explicitly alternate route. An independent socialist party would distinguish its programme from both Pyongyang and foreign patrons, facing intense anti-communist opposition in the South.
COLDWAR_KOR_worker_management_desc: Give workplace councils managerial authority, accepting slower investment decisions. Worker councils would share authority over hiring and production with managers, making investment choices more representative and less centralized.
COLDWAR_KOR_strategic_public_sector_desc: Nationalize strategic credit and infrastructure without absorbing every small enterprise. State ownership of credit, infrastructure and selected heavy industries retains public direction without absorbing neighborhood firms and small producers.
COLDWAR_KOR_industrial_councils_desc: Coordinate sector-wide worker management under a public investment plan. Sector councils bring labor, engineers and public officials into industrial planning, trading managerial discretion for coordinated bargaining.
COLDWAR_KOR_public_holding_fund_desc: Concentrate capital in publicly owned industrial holdings with explicit financial exposure. A public fund would hold strategic stakes and direct reinvestment, concentrating capital under parliamentary scrutiny and carrying market risk on the public balance sheet.
COLDWAR_KOR_southern_socialism_desc: Southern socialists would open dialogue with Pyongyang on coexistence while maintaining their own institutions. The approach asks Northern leaders to negotiate with a pluralist southern government rather than accept its terms in advance.
COLDWAR_KOR_independent_left_public_acco: A socialist government would report public holdings and reinvestment decisions to workers and the Assembly. The disclosures test whether collective ownership delivers accountable stewardship instead of a new circle of insiders.
COLDWAR_KOR_revolutionary_cabinet_desc: An underground movement becomes a government only after a resolved revolutionary or political transition. This is a difficult alternate history. Only a successful revolutionary rupture could bring this underground current into government, leaving it to build authority amid institutional collapse.
COLDWAR_KOR_southern_front_desc: Broaden the revolutionary coalition while protecting a separate Southern government. A broad southern coalition would unite labor, students and civic groups around a separate government, rather than presume agreement on unification.
COLDWAR_KOR_vanguard_party_desc: Centralize the revolution under a disciplined party-state. A disciplined vanguard would centralize authority in party committees, subordinating independent unions and civic organizations to revolutionary leadership.
COLDWAR_KOR_pluralist_socialism_desc: Accept independent socialist and civic representation rather than a monopoly party. Pluralist socialists would keep labor, civic groups and rival left organizations legally active, accepting slower coordination than a monopoly party.
COLDWAR_KOR_party_cadres_desc: Embed cadres in workplaces while accepting coercion and managerial interference. Cadre placement gives party officials influence inside factories, but risks disrupting production and alienating skilled managers and workers.
COLDWAR_KOR_revolutionary_reconstruction: Rebuild production under a public investment guarantee. A public guarantee for reconstruction would direct scarce capital toward damaged productive capacity, increasing state exposure to repayment and project failure.
COLDWAR_KOR_confederal_revolution_desc: Offer Pyongyang a sovereign confederation. The other Korea may reject every constitutional concession. A confederal proposal leaves each Korean government sovereign and requires Pyongyang's explicit agreement on institutions and security.
COLDWAR_KOR_northern_alignment_desc: Seek a Northern security compact at the cost of external access and policy autonomy. A security compact with Pyongyang would recast Southern diplomacy and defense, likely narrowing access to American and other allied support.
COLDWAR_KOR_southern_guarantees_desc: Entrench separate Southern institutions inside an accepted inter-Korean framework. Southern parties would seek enforceable protection for their institutions before accepting a wider inter-Korean framework.
COLDWAR_KOR_joint_planning_desc: Coordinate selected industrial plans after bilateral agreement, without a free transfer of territory. Bilateral planning could coordinate selected industries and transport only after both governments agree on scope, financing and oversight.
COLDWAR_KOR_southern_settlement_desc: Ratify the Southern settlement; any eventual unified state still requires both players’ approval. Ratification would bind Southern parties to agreed terms, while any later unified constitution remains subject to the North's consent.
COLDWAR_KOR_revolutionary_diplomacy_desc: A revolutionary government would seek recognition from states willing to engage its new authorities. Diplomatic standing would depend on each capital's assessment of the government's legitimacy, security commitments and treatment of foreign interests.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_cabinet_desc: A security agency governing directly is an exceptional alternate outcome, not the normal Park starting government. Direct KCIA leadership would replace ordinary cabinet responsibility with intelligence authority, an exceptional outcome shaped by elite and security politics.
COLDWAR_KOR_internal_directorate_desc: Concentrate domestic intelligence and political surveillance. A domestic directorate would prioritize political files, informants and surveillance, bringing civil associations under closer state scrutiny.
COLDWAR_KOR_external_service_desc: Redirect resources toward counterintelligence and external threats. Foreign intelligence and counterintelligence receive greater attention, reserving fewer personnel for monitoring domestic political groups.
COLDWAR_KOR_national_files_desc: Central records improve surveillance while extending arbitrary state power. Centralized files help agencies connect investigations, but also preserve sensitive records that can be used against lawful opponents.
COLDWAR_KOR_warranted_operations_desc: Professional safeguards limit political operations and require oversight. Judicial warrants distinguish criminal and counterintelligence work from partisan surveillance, requiring investigators to document their grounds.
COLDWAR_KOR_counter_infiltration_desc: Border intelligence would connect field reporting with military and police assessments of infiltration risks. The arrangement prioritizes warning and information exchange along the armistice line.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_technocrats_desc: Protect a technocratic cabinet through the security apparatus. Security guarantees shield economic ministers from factional pressure, but risk making policy dependent on secret-police protection.
COLDWAR_KOR_civilian_exit_desc: Negotiate safeguards for a return to civilian politics. A negotiated timetable would return cabinet authority to civilians while asking security officials to accept defined protections and oversight.
COLDWAR_KOR_protected_planning_desc: Guarantee strategic planning at a political and financial cost. Protected ministries can maintain long-term industrial plans through political shocks, at higher financing cost and with weaker public accountability.
COLDWAR_KOR_disclose_archives_desc: Accept a controlled disclosure process and the loss of political intelligence assets. Controlled release would let families and investigators examine selected political cases, sacrificing some intelligence secrecy for public credibility.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_settlement_desc: Institutionalize security responsibilities under the chosen governing settlement. A settlement assigns intelligence and policing powers to specified offices, giving legislators and citizens a clearer account of responsibility.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_handover_desc: Offer a concrete transition compact. A change of government ends this directorate’s active programme. A written compact would define security officials' place during transfer and identify which protections a civilian successor must honor.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_civilian_cabinet_desc: A civilian conservative government combines administrative experience with the contested legacy of the 1961 order. His presidential office is alternate history, grounded in his actual conservative party and prime-ministerial career. Kim Jong-pil's party would draw on conservative organization and administrative experience, while his 1961 coup legacy would complicate claims to civilian legitimacy.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_coalition_desc: Build a parliamentary conservative coalition without a return to presidential emergency rule. A parliamentary coalition can mobilize conservative legislators without reviving the emergency presidential arrangements associated with the DRP.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_executive_desc: Preserve executive coordination while accepting suspicions of the old governing networks. A coordinated executive can speed infrastructure and investment decisions, but cabinet partners may fear Kim Jong-pil is recreating old party networks.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_coalition_committees_des: Share parliamentary authority and preserve a civilian political organization. Coalition committees give partners a role in drafting and oversight, trading unilateral executive control for dependable legislative votes.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_professional_cabinet_des: Professional ministers coordinate development under a strong civilian executive. Technocrats and career administrators would execute a conservative programme under civilian ministers, with ministers answerable to party allies.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_provincial_credit_desc: Invest in Chungcheong without a permanent regional loyalty bonus. Credit for Chungcheong firms and infrastructure answers demands from a region often overshadowed by the southeast's export concentration.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_small_enterprise_desc: Broaden credit access beyond dominant industrial groups. Small manufacturers gain financing and procurement access, reducing reliance on conglomerates without dismantling established industrial groups.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_large_industry_desc: Preserve industrial scale through negotiated state guarantees. Negotiated guarantees preserve large-scale projects in steel, shipbuilding and machinery, leaving public finances exposed if returns disappoint.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_supplier_networks_desc: Give provincial suppliers access to procurement and enforceable contracts. Procurement rules would connect regional workshops to major exporters, making timely payment and quality enforcement central to the bargain.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_export_compromise_desc: Combine export targets and executive bargaining with larger financial exposure. An export compact trades state finance and firm commitments for foreign sales, with borrowing and labor demands shared across participants.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_party_settlement_desc: Consolidate an independent civilian conservative party; a 1990-style merger remains a separate political bargain. A civilian conservative party would build an independent electoral base; any merger with rival parties needs a separate negotiated bargain.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_korean_policy_desc: Offer practical working contacts while preserving separate Southern institutions. Working-level contacts could lower tension and facilitate exchange, while both governments retain their separate claims and security systems.
COLDWAR_KOR_drp_budget_charter_desc: Publish the development budget and subject credit guarantees to a defined approval process. A published charter subjects development accounts and public guarantees to defined review, limiting the discretion of presidential brokers.
COLDWAR_KOR_drp_technocrats_desc: Give the planners professional discretion while limiting presidential patronage. Professional planners would receive authority to set technical standards and monitor results, reducing the role of personal favors.
COLDWAR_KOR_drp_provincial_brokers_desc: Trade central discretion for provincial cooperation and funded rural administration. County officials and provincial notables can secure rural projects, but bargaining ties distribution to local political influence.
COLDWAR_KOR_ndp_tax_transparency_desc: An NDP audit would expose exemptions and connected beneficiaries hidden in the tax system. Ministry accounting and a defensible public record make the review credible, while established firms and political patrons may resist disclosure.
COLDWAR_KOR_ndp_tax_compromise_desc: The NDP can preserve factory investment through negotiated rates and predictable obligations. This accommodation protects exporters from abrupt changes but leaves less immediate revenue for debt reduction and wider social provision.
COLDWAR_KOR_ndp_municipal_services_desc: County administrations would gain funds for roads, water and basic services, giving rural residents more visible benefits. The programme builds local capacity ahead of the later restoration of municipal elections.
COLDWAR_KOR_reform_party_accounts_desc: Make reform-party financing accountable without granting popularity or selecting the election winner. Disclosure of party accounts would make donors and expenditures visible to voters, constraining the patronage finance of every faction.
COLDWAR_KOR_ys_civilian_contracts_desc: Use competitive contracts and disclosure to constrain the old patronage networks. Competitive bids make public contracts harder to steer toward political allies, demanding competent procurement review across ministries.
COLDWAR_KOR_dj_social_dialogue_desc: Bring employers, independent unions and excluded provinces into a funded social bargain. Employers, unions and provincial representatives would negotiate wages and services together, exchanging recurring public support for labor peace.
COLDWAR_KOR_reform_lawful_succession_des: Bind the reform government to the same rules that made its accession possible. The other reform leader may govern later. The same electoral rules must apply when today's reform leaders leave office, reassuring opponents that change will not become another personal monopoly.
COLDWAR_KOR_army_constitutional_service_: Define the legal duties of the armed forces under the actual constitutional settlement. The constitution would define military duties and place deployment under lawful civilian authority, preserving defense readiness within political limits.
COLDWAR_KOR_army_civilian_ministry_desc: Put ministerial appointments under lawful civilian authority; command adaptation has a short-run cost. A civilian defense minister would set personnel and procurement policy, requiring officers to adapt to political rather than club-based appointments.
COLDWAR_KOR_army_advisory_council_desc: Retain formal military advice while accepting a slower and politically contested civilianization. An advisory council preserves professional military input but gives civilian ministers the final word on national policy.
COLDWAR_KOR_usp_national_wage_floor_desc: Set an enforceable minimum floor, accepting costs in low-margin export firms. A legal wage floor raises standards in low-paid sectors, particularly export workshops competing on labor costs.
COLDWAR_KOR_usp_sectoral_bargaining_desc: Negotiate sector agreements that suit different industries, accepting uneven coverage and administrative complexity. Industry agreements let unions and employers set terms for different sectors, demanding state mediators able to resolve uneven coverage.
COLDWAR_KOR_student_workplace_alliance_d: Student organizations and workplace unions would coordinate civic campaigns around education, wages and political rights. Their cooperation draws on shared opposition to restrictions while leaving each movement's leadership and demands intact.
COLDWAR_KOR_left_public_procurement_desc: Give public enterprises accountable procurement instead of insider allocation. Public firms would award contracts under published criteria, limiting favoritism while exposing state enterprises to closer scrutiny.
COLDWAR_KOR_civic_association_law_desc: Protect plural civic associations as a national legal institution that survives ordinary cabinet changes. A general law protects church, student, labor and neighborhood associations, extending legal space beyond parties represented in the Assembly.
COLDWAR_KOR_rpr_worker_elections_desc: Give workers an independent say in public enterprises, at a cost to central directive power. Employees of public enterprises would elect workplace representatives, sharing decisions without transferring every management function to the state.
COLDWAR_KOR_rpr_production_cadres_desc: Concentrate production authority in party cadres, accepting legitimacy and credit costs. Party cadres would direct factories and labor discipline, giving the revolutionary leadership control while risking resentment among skilled workers.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_due_process_desc: Judicial warrants would require agencies to state the grounds for surveillance and operations before acting. Review procedures preserve investigations while giving courts a basis to challenge political misuse.
COLDWAR_KOR_security_protected_archives_: Retain extensive classified political files at the cost of public trust and police expenditure. The directorate keeps political records closed to public review, preserving intelligence sources while prolonging families' uncertainty about state abuses.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_coalition_broker_desc: Trade a distinct party identity for influence inside a negotiated governing coalition. Kim Jong-pil's negotiators can trade committee posts and policy concessions for coalition support, weakening the distinct identity of his party.
COLDWAR_KOR_kjp_independent_party_desc: Preserve an independent conservative organization and accept reduced executive leverage. An independent party can appeal directly to conservative voters, giving up the leverage that comes from joining a larger coalition.
COLDWAR_KOR_constitutional_question_desc: The constitutional review would examine how executive authority, legislative scrutiny and judicial protection should be balanced. A public dossier gives opposing parties and civic organizations a common basis for debate.
COLDWAR_KOR_electoral_opening_desc: Use a genuine electoral or constitutional contest to negotiate enforceable limits on the incumbent. An actual contest or constitutional crisis gives the incumbent reason to negotiate limits, with opposition pressure shaping the terms.
COLDWAR_KOR_interim_cabinet_desc: Support Choi Kyu-hah’s historical caretaker window, or an explicitly negotiated civilian succession. Formal office and coercive command remain separate. Choi Kyu-hah's caretaker office could convene civilian leaders, but it did not command every armed unit during the succession crisis.
COLDWAR_KOR_negotiated_withdrawal_desc: Open talks with a military-led government under organized civilian pressure; no date or party popularity alone completes the handover. Military leaders would need credible guarantees and a timetable to leave executive office as civilian pressure rises.
COLDWAR_KOR_bind_incumbent_desc: Obtain a binding commitment to constitutional talks rather than a personal promise of reform. A public undertaking ties the incumbent to talks that can be tested by legislators, civic leaders and the armed forces.
COLDWAR_KOR_defend_civil_command_desc: Resolve the officer challenge to legitimate command. A failed Seoul Spring may lead to renewed military rule and a later opening. Civilian authority depends on officers following lawful orders; command resistance can reopen the path to martial rule.
COLDWAR_KOR_retirement_guarantees_desc: Offer funded retirement guarantees to remove officers from executive politics. The pension obligation survives an ordinary cabinet change. Pension guarantees give senior officers a material reason to leave political posts, while obliging future governments to honor the terms.
COLDWAR_KOR_authorize_talks_desc: Authorize talks with a real mandate and a resolved command or retirement bargain. A negotiating mandate lets civilian delegates address constitutional rules after command disputes and retirement terms are settled.
COLDWAR_KOR_open_civic_space_desc: Restore lawful meetings, political organization and access to constitutional debate; no party receives free votes. Legal meetings and associations allow churches, students, unions and opposition politicians to organize without prior security permission.
COLDWAR_KOR_broad_democratic_coalition_d: Bring parliamentary opposition, religious groups, students and workers into a negotiating forum without pretending they are one party. Religious networks, opposition figures, students and workers can press for common rules while retaining distinct agendas and leadership.
COLDWAR_KOR_open_security_records_desc: Preserve records of emergency rule and state violence. If Gwangju or other repression occurred, their cases enter this process. Preserving records enables later hearings into emergency decrees, YH and Bu-Ma, and any other documented abuses.
COLDWAR_KOR_unity_ticket_desc: Kim Young-sam and Kim Dae-jung could negotiate one presidential ticket and a shared campaign platform. Agreement would require each leader's supporters to settle questions of nomination, regional representation and future party influence.
COLDWAR_KOR_independent_tickets_desc: Kim Young-sam and Kim Dae-jung could run separate campaigns with distinct organizations and policy appeals. Their choice preserves each movement's leadership, but divides the opposition vote in a direct contest.
COLDWAR_KOR_independent_inquiry_desc: Investigate responsibility through civilian evidence and due process, at administrative and security-transition cost. Civilian investigators would gather testimony and records under due process, risking conflict with security officials and former commanders.
COLDWAR_KOR_conditional_amnesty_desc: Trade limited, conditional guarantees and disclosure for officer cooperation. Credibility and accountability remain contested. Limited immunity could secure testimony and cooperation, but victims and opposition legislators may reject protection without full disclosure.
COLDWAR_KOR_negotiating_mandate_desc: Reconcile the electoral pact and accountability terms before agreeing a constitutional model. Delegates must reconcile electoral coordination with accountability demands before asking the public to ratify a new charter.
COLDWAR_KOR_presidential_democracy_desc: Retain an effective directly elected presidency under binding rights, term and oversight limits. A directly elected president retains executive initiative, constrained by civil rights, term rules and legislative oversight.
COLDWAR_KOR_one_term_presidency_desc: Limiting the presidency to a single term would deny any officeholder a constitutional route to indefinite rule. The administration must pursue its programme within a fixed mandate, while its party prepares a successor capable of winning support in their own right.
COLDWAR_KOR_parliamentary_democracy_desc: Make the cabinet responsible to an elected Assembly. This is an alternate settlement grounded in Korean parliamentary experience and constitutional debates. An Assembly-backed cabinet suits party bargaining and Korea's earlier parliamentary experience, while making governing coalitions vulnerable to division.
COLDWAR_KOR_cabinet_responsibility_desc: Under parliamentary government, ministers would remain in office only while they command Assembly confidence. Coalition bargaining becomes central, and a split among governing parties can bring down the cabinet.
COLDWAR_KOR_consensus_presidency_desc: Retain direct election while binding executive action to a broad cabinet and parliamentary bargain. This is an alternate compromise, not the historical 1987 constitution. Direct election continues, but cabinet consultation and legislative assent would constrain presidential power beyond the 1987 model.
COLDWAR_KOR_coalition_veto_rules_desc: Constitutional amendments would require assent from coalition partners as well as the governing majority. The safeguard prevents one faction rewriting the settlement, but gives smaller parties leverage to delay change.
COLDWAR_KOR_constitution_referendum_desc: Voters would decide whether to ratify the negotiated constitutional text. A public campaign gives both supporters and opponents a direct role in settling the country's institutional design.
COLDWAR_KOR_impartial_election_board_des: Restore lawful electoral competition using the actual party and coalition system; the result may return Roh, either Kim, or another eligible government. An independent commission would administer registration, campaigning and counts, giving competing parties confidence in the ballot.
COLDWAR_KOR_uncensored_press_desc: Protect publication and criticism. These legal rules have enforcement and rollback conditions, not an invented press-freedom meter. Editors and broadcasters could report criticism without prior censorship, allowing voters to hear competing claims before elections.
COLDWAR_KOR_accountable_intelligence_des: Separate external intelligence from political surveillance and require warrants and civilian review. Warrants and legislative review separate foreign intelligence from domestic political policing, limiting secret agencies' authority over opponents.
COLDWAR_KOR_independent_constitutional_c: Create enforceable constitutional review of exceptional powers. The court is a national institution, not a party-specific research bonus. A constitutional court can review emergency authority and rights disputes, giving citizens a remedy beyond legislative negotiation.
COLDWAR_KOR_civilian_appointments_desc: Elected ministers would approve senior military appointments under law, making command selection answerable to the civilian government. The change asks officers to adapt to review beyond established networks.
COLDWAR_KOR_retire_political_networks_de: Officers whose influence rests on political patronage can obstruct civilian authority long after a new constitution is signed. Accelerated retirement would break that continuity through a costly pension settlement, accepting a temporary disruption in command as a new generation assumes responsibility.
COLDWAR_KOR_staged_officer_retirement_de: Preserve near-term command continuity through phased retirement, larger pension obligations and an enforceable review timetable. A review timetable and gradual departures retain near-term command experience, but extend the period of institutional transition.
COLDWAR_KOR_parliamentary_audits_desc: Restore legislative scrutiny over public finance and state abuses, including hearings when the historical cases exist. Assembly hearings expose public spending and state abuses, providing a forum for cases that can be substantiated by records.
COLDWAR_KOR_restore_labour_bargaining_de: Establish lawful independent representation and then use the actual MD labor-faction opinion effect. Existing faction state is never reset. Independent workplace representation gives unions a lawful voice, while employers adjust to bargaining beyond the state-linked federation.
COLDWAR_KOR_prepare_local_councils_desc: Restore the legal basis and timetable for local councils. Historical council elections in 1991 and executive elections in 1995 remain outside this horizon. A legal timetable prepares elected local councils, extending municipal accountability without moving their later elections into this period.
COLDWAR_KOR_constitutional_security_desc: Bind public security to constitutional law. Legal civilian control is distinct from removing every military-era political network. Security services would operate under constitutional law and civilian review, while military-era patronage networks remain a separate problem.
COLDWAR_KOR_orderly_handover_desc: Recognize an actual lawful election and transfer. The constitutional branch never appoints a predetermined winner. A verified election and transfer establish that office changes through lawful procedure, regardless of which eligible candidate wins.
COLDWAR_KOR_defend_new_order_desc: Require lawful authorization for emergency powers and a recorded public constitutional process for reversal. A coup or rollback can still occur, with explicit costs. Emergency powers require legal authorization and public review, making any later rollback visible and politically costly.
